final_answer:
The reasons for taking away Black people's voting rights in the United States include:

1. The Reconstruction Era Amendments (13th, 14th, and 15th) were passed in the aftermath of the Civil War to abolish slavery, grant citizenship to African Americans, and give them the right to vote. However, these amendments were not fully enforced, and many states implemented poll taxes, literacy tests, and other discriminatory measures to prevent Black people from exercising their right to vote.
2. The Jim Crow era (1877-1965) saw the implementation of laws and policies that further restricted voting rights for Black people. These included literacy tests, poll taxes, grandfather clauses, and the use of violence and intimidation to suppress Black voter turnout.
3. The Voting Rights Act of 1965, which prohibited racial discrimination in voting, was an important step towards restoring voting rights for Black Americans. However, the Act did not immediately eliminate all forms of discrimination, and some states continued to enforce restrictive voting laws.

Sources:

1. "Reconstruction Amendments." Encyclopedia Britannica, <https://www.britannica.com/event/Reconstruction-Amendments>.
2. "Jim Crow Laws." Encyclopedia Britannica, <https://www.britannica.com/topic/Jim-Crow-laws>.
3. "Voting Rights Act of 1965." Encyclopedia Britannica, <https://www.britannica.com/event/Voting-Rights-Act-of-1965>.
